issues.quote: I looked at Rosa's kitchen clock when Madame's piano began. It showed two minutes to eleven. When the piano stopped, Rosa's kitchen clock showed eleven minutes past eleven.
issues.fact: L5 names the clock as "Rosa's clock", the same object the master was holding in L4. The transcript changes it to "Rosa's kitchen clock" in L5, which could be read as a different clock from the one in the master's hands.
issues.misreading: A solver could reasonably conclude there are two Rosa clocks, one the master handled that afternoon and a separate kitchen clock she read at 10:58 and 11:11. That would break the link between the master's handling of the clock and the readings she took.

issues.quote: The low notes are the hours. Each quarter is a doubled note, and the minutes past the quarter are high notes, quick and light. He wanted it to strike the first minute of the new century.
issues.fact: The fact sheet says nothing about a repeater, its sound, or how it marks time. This passage gives a sound-based timekeeping method the sheet does not contain.
issues.misreading: A solver could treat the repeater's chime as an independent way to read the hour and quarter from sound, and reinterpret the bell and clock readings or the master's handling of the watches through it.

issues.quote: It is an old joke between him and the clock, and I do not think it has anything to do with this.
issues.fact: L2 says only that the master said what he always says about the hall clock. The witness's characterisation of the remark as a joke and as irrelevant is not in the sheet.
issues.misreading: A solver could dismiss the master's remark about the hall clock as harmless banter and stop considering whether it bears on the clock's reading at ten.

issues.quote: Mine was exact. I regulated it myself, so I knew it would be.
issues.fact: The sheet says only that her watch was exact. It gives no information about who regulated it.
issues.misreading: The added claim that she regulated her own watch could suggest she had reason to know its accuracy independently, which the sheet does not establish.

issues.fact: The sheet describes the watch-showing at dinner only as an event that night. It gives no information about it being a yearly routine.
issues.misreading: A solver could read this as a regular ritual and infer that the master's conduct that night was ordinary, not a deliberate test.

issues.quote: and the master remarked on it.
issues.fact: The sheet says only that Girard would not take his watch out of his pocket. It does not say the master commented on this.
issues.misreading: A solver could read the master's remark as a reaction that signals suspicion or a specific motive.

issues.quote: I noticed that, because the master was particular about it.
issues.fact: The sheet says the regulator agreed with the bell, with no reason given for her noticing it.
issues.misreading: The added reason for her attention could suggest that the agreement mattered to the master in a way the sheet does not state.

issues.quote: I was waiting for something, though I did not know what.
issues.fact: L6 and L5 record only that she stayed in the kitchen and watched the clock. The sheet gives no reason for her waiting and no sense of what she expected.
issues.misreading: A solver could read this as evidence she knew of a planned event, which would shift the timing of the events she describes.

issues.quote: I helped with the hairsprings, and I know what that cost him.
issues.fact: The sheet does not mention hairsprings or her help with the atelier work.
issues.misreading: This adds a personal connection to the master's work and a motive-laden tone that the sheet does not support.

issues.fact: The sheet gives no length of service.
issues.misreading: A solver could take the duration as a fact about how long she has known the master's habits.

issues.quote: Only that my own watch is exact, and that the master would have wanted you to know it.
issues.fact: The sheet records only that her own watch was exact. It says nothing about what the master would have wanted.
issues.misreading: The unsupported claim about the master's wishes could be read as a hint that the master expected a particular account of the time to be given.
